title: Find Valid Matrix Given Row and Column Sums
statement:
You are given two arrays of non-negative integers, `rowSum` and `colSum`. Build a matrix with `rowSum.length` rows and `colSum.length` columns whose entries are all non-negative integers, such that the entries of row `i` add up to `rowSum[i]` and the entries of column `j` add up to `colSum[j]`.

Return any matrix with these properties; several may exist and each one is accepted. The input always admits at least one (in particular, both arrays have the same total).
notes:
## Intuition

Any cell can take at most the smaller of what its row and its column still need. Putting exactly that amount there is always safe: it finishes the row or the column (or both), and what remains is the same kind of problem, one row or column smaller, with the two remaining totals still equal. Starting in the top-left corner and always stepping past the finished line walks a staircase path from the corner to the bottom-right, and every cell off that path stays 0.

## Approach

1. Copy the targets into `rowLeft` and `colLeft` (what each line still needs) and start an all-zero `matrix`.
2. Put `i` on the first row and `j` on the first column.
3. While both are inside the matrix, set `value` to the smaller of `rowLeft[i]` and `colLeft[j]`, write it into `matrix[i][j]` and subtract it from both.
4. If row `i` is now satisfied, move to the next row; otherwise column `j` is, so move to the next column.
5. When either index runs off the end, every line is satisfied because the totals were equal; return `matrix`.

## Example 1, step by step

`rowLeft = [3, 8]`, `colLeft = [4, 7]`. At `(0, 0)`, `value = 3`: row 0 is done, `colLeft = [1, 7]`, so `i = 1`. At `(1, 0)`, `value = 1`: column 0 is done, `rowLeft = [0, 7]`, so `j = 1`. At `(1, 1)`, `value = 7` finishes both and `i = 2` ends the loop. The answer is `[[3, 0], [1, 7]]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(m × n) to build the zero matrix; the loop itself takes at most m + n - 1 steps.
- Space: O(m × n) for the answer, O(m + n) for the copies.

## Pitfalls

- Writing `rowSum[i]` instead of the smaller of the two needs can push a column over its target.
- When a row and a column finish together, advance only one index; the next cell simply gets 0.
- Do not stop as soon as one line is done; keep going until an index leaves the matrix.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `rowLeft`, `colLeft` | how much each row and column still needs |
| `matrix` | the answer, all zeros except along the path |
| `i`, `j` | the current row and column |
| `value` | amount placed in the current cell |

narration.2: Copy the row targets; this array tracks what each row still needs.
narration.3: Do the same for the columns.
narration.4: Start from an all-zero matrix of the right shape.
narration.8: Walk while the current cell is inside the matrix.
narration.9: The cell can hold at most what both its row and its column still need.
narration.10: Place that amount in the cell.
narration.11: The row now needs that much less...
narration.13: If the row is satisfied, nothing more goes in it...
narration.14: ...so move down to the next row.
narration.16: Otherwise the column is satisfied, so move right to the next column.
narration.19: Every row and column now has its exact total.
